January 2013
# Economic Focus **Chinese growth bouncing back** China's GDP grew 7.8% in 2012, the slowest annual growth since 1999. While China seems to be transitioning to a period of structurally slower growth, much of last year’s slowdown was due to cyclical factors. Looking ahead, the latest data suggest China’s economy is now entering a cyclical upturn; Q4 2012 GDP growth reached 7.9% year on year, up from 7.4% in Q3. We expect the pace of economic growth to continue to accelerate through the first half of 2013, driven by improvements in the property market and robust consumption. Continued acceleration through the second half of the year however is less certain. ## **Nominal growth in real estate investment Construction investment growth by region** 35% 40%

**The foundations of recovery** As in any economy, growth cycles are driven by a multitude of factors. In our view the most influential driver of China’s economic cycle is the real estate market. Faced with rapid house price appreciation and falling housing affordability for the masses, China's government enacted a number of measures aimed at cooling the real estate market in early 2011. While these measures were successful in cooling house prices, they also resulted in faltering construction activity. As can be seen in the chart above, real estate investment growth slowed sharply in 2012, dropping to the lows endured through 2009. While the downturn in real estate was evident across all China, it was most pronounced in the coastal East where the property market is more mature and prices are typically higher. Aside from the direct impact on total GDP (real estate accounts for around 25% of total investment), the slowdown in the real estate market has had knock-on implications for many associated industries such as raw materials and white goods. There is no doubt that the slowdown in real estate led to a deceleration in GDP growth through 2012. But now the foundation has been set for a recovery in housing, with positive implications for GDP growth in 2013. **If the price is right…** The first signs of a recovery in house building began to emerge last summer. House prices across much of China stopped falling, and in many areas started to g

radually increase. Falling prices acted as a disincentive for developers to build – new housing started in urban areas fell 13% year on year in the first three quarters of 2012. In addition, we suspect falling prices resulted in some households delaying purchases in anticipation of further price declines. The return to house price growth is gradually feeding through into construction activity; new starts in Q4 2012 were down by just 2% on a year earlier. We have also seen a sharp rebound in sales. House price growth gained momentum at the end of 2012, and we expect this to contribute to a return to growth in new housing construction in 2013. This will filter through into wider industry, providing a boost to the economy as a whole. ## **Annual growth in housing floor space completed and sold** 50%

**Further government intervention?** Government policy remains an uncertainty that could hinder the recovery. The measures introduced by the government in early 2011 were designed to curb speculation in the property market. Overseas capital flows were restricted and the purchase of second homes required larger down-payments. In some areas, limits were placed on the number of homes a family could own. By limiting price gains, the government hoped to improve housing affordability for the majority. In this light, the recent rise in house prices may prompt further restrictions, particularly the price rise accelerates. The fundamentals of the market suggest that price gains may not be excessive through the first half of 2013, as housing supply is ample. The chart above shows that in the past two years we have seen rapid growth in volume of housing completed, as properties started in the boom years have been finished and brought to market. Sales growth, by contrast, has been weak. In short, in 2011 and 2012 supply growth outstripped demand growth, reversing the trend of previous years. But as we move into the second half of 2013 growth in housing Metals Market Service Monthly Update - January 2013 Page 2 of 6 Economic Focus completions will slow (significantly), – the result of weaker construction volumes in the past couple of years – while sales growth will continue its recent trend of acceleration. Upward pressure on house prices will likely increase. **GDP growth picks up in 2013** Rising house prices, together with an upturn in consumer price inflation that has become apparent in the past few months, could trigger a tightening in government policies in the second half of 2013. Whether such tightening takes the form of rising interest rates or measures targeted specifically at real estate is hard to say, but keeping housing affordability from rapidly worsening is likely to remain a priority for the gove

rnment. In either case, policy tightening would have a cooling effect on overall economic growth. Wood Mackenzie forecasts Chinese GDP growth to accelerate in H1 2013, driven by the housing market in particular. Into H2, we expect growth to gradually slow, generating annual growth in 2013 of 8.4%. ## **Quarterly GDP growth in China (year on year %)** 16%
